# Introduction

Package **growthrates** comes with a set of built-in parametric growth models
that should be sufficient for many application scenarios, though of course not
under all circumstances. This document describes how the set of available
functions can be extended with your own user-defined models. Section 3
describes how simple regression functions existing in *closed form* can be
implemented. Section 4 shows how growth models defined by systems of ordinary
differential equations (ODEs) can be implemented directly in R, and finally
Section 5 describes how ODE models can be implemented as inline C code.

# Differential equations or closed form?

Growth models can be either "ordinary functions" of time $f(t)$ in *closed
form*—allowing you to obtain values for the dependent variable $y$
immediately from any given value of an independent variable $t$ (or `time`)
without iteration—or differential equation models $dy/dt$ that require
numerical integration.

Sometimes a model can be written in either form. For example, the logistic
growth model can be expressed as a differential equation:

$$\frac{dy}{dt} = \mu_{\max} \cdot y \left(1 - \frac{y}{K}\right)$$

or as its analytical solution in closed form:

$$y(t) = \frac{K \cdot y_0}{y_0 + (K - y_0) \cdot e^{-\mu_{\max} \cdot t}}$$

The second form is much easier to evaluate because $y$ can be computed
directly from $t$, whereas the first version requires either analytical
integration (yielding the second form) or numerical simulation of how $y$
evolves stepwise over time.

On the other hand, models formulated as differential equations are often more
directly tied to a mechanistic process description and easier to extend.

# Growth models in closed form

Suppose we want to extend the logistic growth model with an additional shift
parameter along the $y$-axis, for example because part of the population does
not participate in growth. This leads to an equation of the form:

$$y(t) = \frac{K \cdot y_0}{y_0 + (K - y_0) \cdot e^{-\mu_{\max} t}} + y_{\text{shift}}$$

After loading package **growthrates**:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
suppressMessages(require("growthrates"))
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
library("growthrates")
```

we can immediately define our own function in the user workspace without
modifying the package itself. To make it compatible with **growthrates**, it is
sufficient to follow the input and output conventions described on the
`?growthmodel` help page.

The function can have any valid name, provided that:

1. it takes exactly two arguments, `time` and `parms`, as input, and
2. its return value is a matrix with at least two columns named `time` and `y`.

The body of the function can be adapted as needed, as long as the mapping
between inputs and outputs makes sense from a scientific perspective.

```{r}
grow_logistic_yshift <- function(time, parms) {
  with(as.list(parms), {
    y <- (K * y0) / (y0 + (K - y0) * exp(-mumax * time)) + y_shift
    data.frame(time = time, y = y) |> as.matrix()
  })
}
```

At first glance, `data.frame(time = time, y = y) |> as.matrix()` may look
roundabout, but it is a straightforward way to produce the required matrix
format.

It is always good practice to test the function beforehand, for example:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-align: center
time <- 1:10
out <- grow_logistic_yshift(time, parms = list(y0 = 1, mumax = 0.5, K = 10, y_shift = 2))
plot(time, out[, "y"], type = "b")
```

Future versions of **growthrates** may introduce additional checks, so it is
already helpful to wrap the function in a constructor of the same name to
create an object of class `growthmodel`:

```r
grow_logistic_yshift <- growthmodel(grow_logistic_yshift,
                                    c("y0", "mumax", "K", "y_shift"))
```

Now the new model is ready to be fitted to test data:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-align: center
x <- seq(5, 100, 5)
y <- c(2.1, 2.3, 5, 4.7, 4.3, 6.9, 8.2, 11.5, 8.8, 10.2, 14.5, 12.5,
       13.6, 12.7, 14.2, 12.5, 13.8, 15.1, 12.7, 14.9)

fit <- fit_growthmodel(grow_logistic_yshift,
                       p = c(y0 = 1, mumax = 0.1, K = 10, y_shift = 1),
                       time = x, y = y)
plot(fit)
summary(fit)
```

# Differential equation models in R

Differential equation models can be used in a similar way, though they are
slightly more involved because:

1. we need two functions: one for the ODE model (the derivatives) and one for
   the numerical integration;
2. an ODE model distinguishes between time-dependent *state variables* and
   constant *parameters*, even though both are treated as *parameters* during
   statistical estimation. This distinction between **statistical parameters**
   (from the perspective of model fitting) and **ODE model parameters** should
   be kept clear; and
3. numerical integration is a broad topic that requires care and experience. A
   concise overview can be found in @Soetaert2010c.

In the example below, we assume that the carrying capacity is a function of
time. This can be represented by a system of two differential equations—one
for the carrying capacity ($K$) and one for population abundance ($y$). For
simplicity, we assume a linear increase in $K$, though more elaborate
formulations are certainly possible, such as biochemical conversion of a mixed
substrate, Monod kinetics on a limiting resource, density dependence, or
semi-continuous nutrient additions.

The growth model consists of two parts:

1. a function `ode_...` defining the differential equations, and
2. a growth model `grow_...` computing the numerical solution.

In the latter, the statistical parameters are split into initial values for the
state variables (`init`) and the ODE model parameters. We also need to keep
initial values (such as $y_0$) distinct from the state variables (such as $y$)
that evolve over time.

```{r}
ode_K_linear <- function(time, init, parms, ...) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, init)), {
    dy <- mumax * y * (1 - y / K)
    dK <- dK
    list(c(dy, dK))
  })
}

grow_K_linear <- function(time, parms, ...) {
  init <- parms[c("y0", "K")]         # initial values
  names(init) <- c("y", "K")           # enforce state variable names
  odeparms <- parms[c("mumax", "dK")]  # ODE model parameters
  out <- ode(init, time, ode_K_linear, parms = odeparms)
  out
}
```

Again, it is wise to test the function first:

```{r}
grow_K_linear <- growthmodel(grow_K_linear,
                             pnames = c("y0", "K", "mumax", "dK"))
grow_K_linear(time = 1:10, c(y0 = 0.1, K = 1, mumax = 0.1, dK = 0.5)) |> head()
```

before fitting the model to data:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: center
x <- seq(5, 100, 5)
y <- c(0.1, 2.2, 3.1, 1.5, 8.9, 8, 8.4, 9.8, 9.3, 10.6, 12, 13.6,
       13.1, 13.3, 11.6, 14.7, 12.6, 13.9, 16.9, 14.4)
fit <- fit_growthmodel(grow_K_linear,
                       p = c(y0 = 0.1, mumax = 0.2, K = 10, dK = 0.1),
                       time = x, y = y)
plot(fit)
summary(fit)
```

# Inline C code with package cOde

Numerical simulation of ODE models can occasionally be slow. Making compiled
code, i.e. writing the model in a language such as C or Fortran that runs faster
than R—an attractive option. Several approaches exist for doing this; see, for
example, @Soetaert2010c, @Kneis2016, and @Kneis2017. Below, we use an
approach that supports *inline code*, integrating C code directly from an R
script via package **cOde** [@Kaschek2016].

Note, however, that compiled code requires appropriate C and/or Fortran
compilers along with developer tools. These are often pre-installed on Linux,
whereas Windows users need to install Rtools from
<https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/>.

```{r}
#| eval: false
## Example of using compiled growth models from inline code via the 'cOde'
## package by Daniel Kaschek.
## Note: This example requires R development tools:
##  - suitable compilers on Linux and macOS
##  - Rtools on Windows from [https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/)

library("growthrates")
library("cOde")

## Define a system of ODEs and compile it --------------------------------------
ode_K_linear <- funC(c(
  y = "mumax * y * (1 - y / K)",
  K = "dK"
))

yini <- c(y = 1, K = 10)
parms <- c(mumax = 0.1, dK = 0.05)

## Run the model
out1 <- odeC(yini, times = 0:100, ode_K_linear, parms = parms)

## Generate synthetic test data with normally distributed noise
x <- seq(5, 100, 5)
y <- odeC(yini, x, ode_K_linear, parms)[, "y"] + rnorm(x)

## Create a 'growthmodel' with interfaces compatible with growthrates
## Consistent names for parameters and initial values are essential!
grow_K_linear <- function(time, parms, ...) {
  init <- parms[c("y0", "K")]  # initial values
  names(init) <- c("y", "K")    # enforce names
  out <- odeC(init, time, ode_K_linear, parms)
  out
}

## Convert to a 'growthmodel' object (may be required by future extensions)
grow_K_linear <- growthmodel(grow_K_linear, pnames = c("y0", "mumax", "K", "dK"))

## Test the growthmodel
## Columns named 'time' and 'y' are mandatory.
grow_K_linear(time = x, c(y0 = 1, mumax = 0.1, K = 10, dK = 0.1)) |> head()

## Fit the model ---------------------------------------------------------------
fit <- fit_growthmodel(grow_K_linear,
                       p = c(y0 = 1, mumax = 0.1, K = 10, dK = 0.1),
                       time = x, y = y)
plot(fit)
summary(fit)

## Unload DLL and clean up -----------------------------------------------------
## DLL creation should ideally be directed to a temporary directory.
dll <- paste(ode_K_linear, .Platform$dynlib.ext, sep = "")
dyn.unload(dll)
unlink(dll)
unlink(paste(ode_K_linear, ".c", sep = ""))
unlink(paste(ode_K_linear, ".o", sep = ""))
```
